paragraphs.heading: A wave made by a falling mass
paragraphs.text: A megatsunami is a huge wave produced when a large quantity of material abruptly drops into water or lands close beside it. Landslides, meteor impacts and volcanic eruptions can all deliver that material. The word was coined by the media and has no exact definition, but people usually use it for tsunamis taller than 100 metres (328 ft).

paragraphs.heading: How ordinary tsunamis behave
paragraphs.text: An ordinary tsunami starts when a powerful earthquake moves the sea floor up or down and shifts the water above it. Out in deep water the wave is low, usually just a slight swell of around 30 centimetres, and it could pass under a ship without the crew noticing. It grows sharply as the sea floor rises toward land. Even so, it typically stays below about 30 metres (100 ft), even after the strongest earthquakes.

paragraphs.heading: Why megatsunamis are so tall
paragraphs.text: A megatsunami is a separate kind of event with a different physical cause. Here the material that pushes the water aside splashes it upward and outward, so the first wave can be hundreds of metres high. Underwater earthquakes and eruptions do not normally do this by themselves, but landslides they set off beside water can, because they push aside far more water. If a slide or impact hits a hemmed-in body of water, as at Lituya Bay in 1958 and the Vajont Dam in 1963, the water may have nowhere to spread, and one or more enormous waves can follow.

paragraphs.heading: Landslide waves fade quickly
paragraphs.text: Waves from landslides tend to have big run-ups close to where they start, run-up being the height the water surges to when it meets land. But they weaken more quickly with distance than earthquake tsunamis do. In Papua New Guinea on 17 July 1998, a landslide tsunami sent waves up to 15 metres high onto 20 kilometres of coast and killed 2,200 people, yet farther away it was not a major danger. A landslide disturbs a fairly small area, which makes waves with shorter wavelengths, and such waves are boosted along nearby coasts but die down as they spread outward.

paragraphs.heading: What sets the size
paragraphs.text: The kind of tsunami a landslide makes depends on the slide's volume, speed, initial acceleration, length and thickness. Volume and initial acceleration matter most in deciding whether a tsunami forms at all, and a sudden stop of the slide can make the waves larger. Slides in shallow water tend to make bigger tsunamis, and shallow water is also usually near the coast, so the wave has less distance to weaken before reaching shore. Giant collapses are rare, which makes it hard to test the models used to simulate these waves.

paragraphs.heading: The tallest waves on record
paragraphs.text: Pinning down a typical height is complex and debated, partly because reports may give the wave's height in open water or its run-up, which can be several times larger. No minimum height is broadly agreed, but the few megatsunamis observed in recent history all had run-ups above 100 metres. The 1980 eruption of Mount St. Helens drove a wave 260 metres up in Spirit Lake, Washington, and the 1958 wave in Lituya Bay climbed 520 metres, the tallest ever recorded. Researchers studying traces of ancient asteroid impacts suggest those may have raised waves over 1,500 metres high.
